thread.title: GPT Live T3 Code Feedback Loops

messages.text: Explain to me how GPT Live 1 works and what we're trying to do to make it work with T3 code. Importantly I want to understand the fastest feedback loops that we can get. So when something should be close to instant like please open me the thread called this thing. If there's a thread called that it should open almost instantaneously.

I’ll look through the project notes and implementation to explain how GPT Live 1 connects to T3 Code, with particular attention to what adds latency to a simple “open this thread” request. I’m applying the unslop skill for the explanation.

The plan has an important latency constraint: GPT Live handles the conversation, but a second model chooses the T3 tools. I’m checking that handoff and the latest live-test results. I’m also using the OpenAI Docs skill to verify the documented behavior.

**Opening a clearly named thread should feel like a voice shortcut.** The current design can do that in principle, but it sends even simple navigation through a second model. We have not yet measured whether that path is fast enough.

GPT Live 1 handles the spoken conversation: listening, speaking, and interruptions. When something requires reasoning or tools, it delegates to a backend. Our configuration uses GPT-5.6 Terra for that backend. OpenAI manages the conversation context and backend connection; T3 executes the requested functions. [Official OpenAI documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation)

For your example, the current path is:

```text
You: "Open the thread called Macroscope trials"
                  ↓
GPT Live recognizes that T3 needs to do something
                  ↓
Terra requests a thread search
                  ↓
T3 returns matching threads
                  ↓
Terra selects one and requests openThread
                  ↓
T3 navigates to it and verifies the destination
                  ↓
GPT Live confirms the result
```

The thread should appear as soon as T3 executes navigation. Spoken confirmation can follow. Waiting for the assistant to finish saying “I found your thread, opening it now” would add unnecessary delay.

What we are building is a voice interface inside T3’s web and desktop app. It can find threads by title or description, explain existing work, open threads across connected environments, and start longer work in ordinary T3 threads. Those workers can continue while you keep talking. The client already owns the connections and navigation, so it can operate T3 directly through its APIs. [MVP plan](/Users/aus-m5p-as/projects/oracle/MVP-PLAN.md:15)

**The biggest opportunity is to give obvious navigation a much shorter path.**

I found a concrete issue in the current implementation: search checks thread titles, but then still waits for message searches before returning. If no environment is specified, it waits for results from all selected environments too. An exact title match currently does not end the search early. [Search implementation](/Users/aus-m5p-as/projects/t3code-oracle-live/apps/web/src/voice/tools.ts:883)

I would distinguish these requests:

| Request | Appropriate execution |
|---|---|
| “Open the thread called X” | Look up the title in the current authorized catalog and navigate when the match is unique. |
| “Open the thread where we discussed X” | Search titles first, then messages if needed. Read candidates only when the result is unclear. |
| “What did we decide about X?” | Retrieve supporting history and generate an answer. |
| “Investigate X” | Start a worker, promptly confirm that it started, and deliver findings later. |

For the first case, I would aim for **under one second from the end of the identifying phrase to the thread appearing**, on a warm connection. That is a proposed target, not a measured capability. Our existing plan allows a three-second median and six-second p95 for find-and-open. That is too loose for the exact-title interaction you describe. [Current targets](/Users/aus-m5p-as/projects/oracle/MVP-PLAN.md:109)

There are two ways to shorten it.

1. **Improve the existing delegation path.** Give the backend one `findAndOpenThread` operation. T3 resolves a unique title and navigates within that call, returning candidates if clarification is needed. This removes the model round trip between “here are the search results” and “open this one.” Keep the catalog current, avoid unnecessary message searches, and tune backend reasoning for this small task.

2. **Use a direct command path for predictable requests.** Recognize “open thread X” from the transcript, resolve X in application code, and navigate without another model deciding which tool to call. GPT Live remains the conversational interface. This requires more application logic for corrections, ambiguity, and preventing duplicate execution. OpenAI’s client delegation mode supports custom routing, but our current MVP deliberately uses managed Responses delegation. [Delegation modes](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation)

I would measure the improved managed path first. OpenAI already keeps its Responses connection persistent and prepares configuration in advance, so it has some latency optimizations built in. Whether those are sufficient for our target needs a real measurement. [Backend latency guidance](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation#reduce-backend-latency)

The fastest development feedback loop is one repeatable request against one known thread, with timestamps for:

- End of the identifying phrase.
- Delegation and tool selection.
- Search completion.
- Correct thread visibly rendered.
- Spoken confirmation actually played.

Run the same navigation directly without voice to establish T3’s baseline. Then run it through voice. That tells us whether the delay comes from speech handling, model handoffs, search, or rendering. An immediate “sure” is not task completion.

The latest recorded test established a working Live connection and speech exchange. It also exposed a failure where Live claimed it lacked access instead of delegating. The frontend instructions were corrected, but successful voice-driven lookup and navigation remain unverified in the latest report. [Live test status](/Users/aus-m5p-as/projects/oracle/campaign/reports/LIVE-DELEGATION-PROMPT-2026-09-14.md:1)

My priority would be to prove and time **one spoken exact-title request opening one real thread**, then remove every unnecessary step from that path.
test that

I’ll test the exact-title request against the isolated T3 instance and measure how quickly the thread opens. I’m using the browser skill to verify the visible result and the unslop skill for reporting.

There is newer evidence than the report I cited: typed requests now open the correct thread through the real backend, and your existing tab shows a spoken September lookup succeeded too. I’ll use a separate test tab to time repeatable exact-title requests. Typed input measures the backend and navigation path; it excludes speech recognition and Live’s decision to delegate.

The first exact-title request opened correctly in **3.82 seconds**. The actual search took only about **44 ms** after the backend response completed; most of the delay came from successive model turns to discover the environment, search, and open. I’m checking a warm follow-up, then I’ll test recorded speech through the audio path.

The recorded-speech test opened the correct thread **4.35 seconds after the audio ended**. Direct sidebar navigation took **55 ms**. Both typed tests also took several seconds, so speech recognition alone is not the bottleneck. I’m saving the timing trace and closing my test session.

**It opens the correct thread, but it is nowhere near instant yet.**

| Test | Time until thread appeared |
|---|---:|
| Direct sidebar click | **55 ms** |
| Typed exact-title request | **3.82 s** |
| Typed follow-up, same session | **4.27 s** |
| Recorded speech through GPT Live | **4.35 s after speech ended** |

The speech test said “Open the thread called Onboarding plan September.” Live understood it and opened September correctly.

Most delay came from successive model turns: discover environments, search threads, then open the match. Search execution took roughly **44–73 ms**. Navigation itself was also fast.

The first change worth testing is **one find-and-open operation**, with a unique title match opening immediately inside that operation. That removes the extra model decision between finding the thread and opening it.

These are individual measurements using synthetic speech and small test threads. [Full results and evidence](/Users/aus-m5p-as/projects/oracle/campaign/reports/LIVE-LATENCY-2026-09-14.md).

Yeah, we want to have almost instant navigation and command work That stuff needs to feel like something similar to just using the mouse. For things like open the thread that does this thing or make me a new thread for this or start a new project for XYZ And I need you to figure out how we can do that while retaining the smartness of the model for more complicated or nuanced tasks as well.

I’ll investigate a faster command path for navigation and creation, while keeping model reasoning available for ambiguous requests. I’ll use the measured delays to compare designs and test the smallest useful prototype.

I’m using the codebase-design and research skills to work out where command handling should live. This will be a bounded investigation on the current model, with no child agents: compare the supported Live options, inspect T3’s creation paths, and produce a measured recommendation.

The research skill calls for a background researcher, so I’m assigning one small documentation task to GPT-5.6 Luna while I inspect T3 locally. The usage guard is clear. I’ll keep the work to this design question.

T3 already has fast paths we can reuse: “New thread” opens a draft without waiting for an agent, and project creation is a direct command. The slower work can follow that visible action.

There is also a limit worth separating from model delay: in our speech test, “September” reached the transcript about **770 ms after the audio ended**. A direct command path could remove several seconds, but getting closer to mouse speed will also require faster recognition of the identifying words.

The small command-planner experiment passed 25 cases, including duplicate titles, negation, corrections, and requests that need model interpretation. Exact lookup over 10,000 cached titles took well under a millisecond; that is only the local lookup cost, not an end-to-end voice result.

The useful split is becoming clear: a request can have a simple action and a complicated task. “Make me a new thread to investigate this migration” can open the thread view promptly while the model works out the investigation. We should not make opening that view wait for the investigation plan.

**We should make voice commands use the same fast actions as the mouse, and use the model only for the parts that need interpretation.** GPT Live can remain the conversational interface.

The key distinction is between understanding the command and doing the work. “Make me a new thread to investigate this migration” has a simple command and a complicated task. Opening the thread should happen promptly; investigating the migration can use the full intelligence of the model afterward.

I recommend this design:

| Request | How it should run |
|---|---|
| “Open the thread called September onboarding” | Resolve the unique title from T3’s current catalog and navigate directly. |
| “Open the thread where we compared code review tools” | Search cached titles and supporting snippets while you speak. Use a model if choosing the correct thread requires interpretation. |
| “Make me a new thread” | Use T3’s existing new-thread action and current defaults. |
| “Make me a new thread to investigate this” | Open the workspace promptly, retain the request and referenced context, then start the appropriate worker once the brief is resolved. |
| “Start a new project called XYZ” | Use the configured environment and project directory, then execute T3’s project-creation command directly. |
| A nuanced or ambiguous request | Give the model the conversation, current workspace and relevant evidence so it can reason or clarify. |

**The model should not have to discover the environment, search, inspect the results, and separately decide to open something we already know.**

There are four changes behind this.

1. **Keep useful context ready.** T3 already knows its thread titles, current project, connected environments and selected model. Keep that information current. For descriptions of older work, prepare searchable, source-linked summaries as threads change instead of generating them when you ask.

2. **Start looking while you speak.** Partial speech can trigger searches and prefetch likely threads. Show candidates early. Commit navigation or creation when the command is sufficiently resolved. “September, actually October” must update the same request.

3. **Give T3 ownership of execution.** I recommend GPT Live’s *client delegation* mode. It lets our application route requests through direct code or a model. The official API also supports processing transcript fragments before delegation arrives. We would need to manage context and backend connections ourselves. [OpenAI delegation documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/live-delegation)

4. **Use one execution record.** Direct commands and model fallback must share the same operation ID and result. That prevents a later model response from opening an old destination or creating a second thread.

I tested a small offline command planner against 25 cases, including duplicates, negation, corrections and contextual requests. Exact lookup over 10,000 cached titles was comfortably below one millisecond. **That proves lookup is cheap, not that voice is now fast.** The integration remains to be built.

There is another bottleneck: our recorded test delivered the identifying word about **770 ms after speech ended**, then spent another **3.58 seconds** reaching navigation. Removing the model turns addresses that second delay. To get closer to mouse speed, we should also benchmark a parallel low-delay transcription stream. OpenAI provides tunable streaming transcription and final input-item events, which would also help us commit creation commands reliably. [Transcription documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-transcription)

My proposed targets are roughly **100 ms once a resolved command is available**, and **300–500 ms after speech ends for clear commands**. The latter is a target to test, not a capability we have established.

I’ve written the [design, implementation sequence and remaining tests](/Users/aus-m5p-as/projects/oracle/research/instant-commands-design.md). The first implementation should cover exact-title navigation and new-thread creation, with intelligent fallback preserved from the start.
sounds good to me, try it out

I’ll build and test the first version: direct exact-title navigation and new-thread opening, with ambiguous requests still going to the model. I’ll keep it on the isolated T3 instance and compare it against the timings we already measured.

I’m making the first trial opt-in so we can compare it with the working voice path. Simple navigation and new-draft requests will execute in T3; other requests will use the existing backend model. This trial will wait for Live’s delegation signal before acting on speech, rather than treating a partial transcript as permission to create or start work.

The first implementation passes its focused tests. Exact titles and “make me a new thread” use the direct path; ambiguous requests still reach the backend model, with prior command results included as context. I’m moving to the live browser test now, including a follow-up that needs interpretation.

The previous test web server had stopped, so I started a fresh instance with its own snapshot of the synthetic data. It is on port 5925. The original environment remains separate; the new trial’s typechecks and focused tests are passing.

The live typed tests are much faster: **130 ms** to open September’s thread and **94 ms** to open a new draft. Neither called the backend model. I’m now checking that an ambiguous onboarding request still gets an intelligent clarification, then repeating the recorded-speech test.

Recorded speech now opens the correct thread in **1.28 seconds after the audio ends**, down from **4.35 seconds**. Nearly all of the remaining wait was before Live delivered the identifying word and delegation signal; T3 then opened the thread in about **150 ms**.

The model also retained the direct action’s context: a follow-up about the onboarding plan correctly recognized that September was already open.
The direct commands are already much faster. I’m finishing the contextual follow-up test now, to verify that “open October instead” still uses the model and reaches the correct thread.

The contextual test passed: “Open October instead” used the model, opened October in 2.70 seconds, and confirmed it afterward. Exact-title navigation on the same build took 120 ms. That gives us the intended split: immediate commands when the destination is certain, model reasoning when interpretation is needed.

Implemented and tested an opt-in prototype.

| Command | Time to visible result |
|---|---:|
| Exact thread title, typed | **120 ms** |
| New thread draft, typed | **94 ms** |
| Exact thread title, spoken | **1.28 s**, previously 4.35 s |
| New thread draft, spoken | **1.62 s** |
| “Open October instead,” using model context | **2.70 s** |

The split works: clear commands execute directly; nuanced requests retain model reasoning and conversation context.

The remaining speech delay is mostly waiting for Live to deliver the command. T3 acts in roughly **100–150 ms** afterward. That speech boundary is the next bottleneck to tackle.

The prototype passed 30 focused tests and both type checks. Project creation is still outside this first trial.

I’m separating three cases: reading an update uses the existing thread’s history; asking its worker for an update sends a message to that thread; creating a thread requires a new-thread request. A missing or ambiguous target must not become a new thread.

For navigation, the chime will happen only after T3 confirms the destination. Failures and questions will still be spoken.

The fixes now pass the focused tests. They cover a deliberately wrong model call: if the user asks an existing thread for an update and the model tries to create a new thread, execution refuses it and returns guidance to use the existing thread.

The new follow-up tool preserves the thread ID, model, workspace, and title. I’m checking the integrated app next, including whether navigation stays silent and produces exactly one chime.

The live check confirms one chime and no spoken confirmation for exact navigation. The update request also selected `continueThread` with the original thread ID.

That test thread’s provider is disabled, so the update correctly failed without creating a replacement. I’m checking the remaining speech behavior and preserving this failure case in the test coverage.

The spoken test caught one more issue: Live still said “Sure, let me find it” despite the silence instruction. I’m adding a playback gate for navigation, so quiet completion does not depend on the model obeying a prompt. The chime stays audible; errors and clarification can still speak.

The replay now opens the thread with one chime. Live generated a backchannel again, but the playback gate kept it muted and out of the visible transcript. The navigation feedback is now enforced by the client.

I’m doing the final check that a normal question can speak again afterward, then I’ll leave the corrected demo ready to reconnect.

Fixed in the [running prototype](http://localhost:5925). Reconnect to try it.

- Navigation now gives one short chime. The client suppresses navigation chatter, even when Live generates it.
- Update requests can continue the existing thread, preserving its history and settings. Creating a replacement is blocked unless explicitly requested.
- Errors, questions, and substantive answers still speak.

Regression tests and type checks pass. Live testing confirmed quiet navigation and correct existing-thread targeting. The demo thread’s disabled provider prevented its update from running, without creating another thread.
